721: D is correct because AWS Lambda natively supports Python, runs custom code without provisioning servers, and scales automatically to handle hundreds of requests per second. Lambda is a truly serverless service, so it requires minimal infrastructure and minimal operational support compared to managing EC2 fleets, Elastic Beanstalk environments, or Kubernetes clusters. This makes it the best fit for testing a microservice in a serverless rearchitecture.
722: A is correct because an AWS Transit Gateway provides central hub-and-spoke connectivity so every attached VPC can communicate with all other VPCs without full-mesh peering. Associating the existing Direct Connect connection with a transit VIF extends on-premises connectivity to every VPC attached to the transit gateway through a single interface. Route propagation automatically populates the VPC route tables, keeping the architecture centrally managed with the least operational overhead.
723: C is correct because Default Host Management Configuration in AWS Systems Manager enables automatic management and patching of EC2 instances without requiring any changes to the IAM roles already attached to the instances. The feature uses a service-linked role, so the existing role the applications rely on for RDS access remains intact and the running applications are not disrupted. It also removes the manual work of creating and attaching roles across the fleet.
724: B is correct because the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler automatically adjusts the number of nodes in the EKS cluster when pods cannot be scheduled because of insufficient capacity, and removes nodes when they are underutilized. This directly resolves the problem of the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scaling pods while node capacity stays fixed. As a purpose-built, fully integrated Kubernetes component, it requires far less administrative effort than custom Lambda logic or manually tracked metrics.
725: B is correct because frequently replaced 50 GB objects uploaded with multipart uploads can leave incomplete multipart upload parts stored in S3, and those orphaned parts keep accruing storage charges even though the completed objects are constant in number and size. An S3 Lifecycle policy that aborts incomplete multipart uploads automatically deletes those parts after a set number of days. This stops the month-over-month cost growth without changing the application's upload pattern.
726: D is correct because Amazon ElastiCache for Redis provides in-memory data storage that can sustain rapid, high-volume reads and writes of player location data at very low latency, absorbing the peak workloads that overwhelm the RDS for PostgreSQL instance. Redis also natively supports geospatial data types and operations that fit latitude and longitude tracking. Offloading the frequent location updates and reads to the cache relieves the database bottleneck while it remains the durable store.
727: C is correct because DynamoDB deletion protection blocks DeleteTable operations entirely, preventing an accidental deletion before it can cause data loss and operational disruption. It is a simple table-level setting that requires no pipelines, scripts, or recovery procedures, so it has the least operational overhead. While point-in-time recovery helps restore a deleted table, deletion protection avoids the loss and downtime in the first place.
728: B is correct because Storage Gateway cached volumes store the primary copy of all data in Amazon S3 while retaining only frequently accessed subsets locally on a cache, which solves the on-premises capacity shortage. Because the recent data is served from the local cache, frequently accessed data is available for immediate retrieval at no additional retrieval cost. Cached volumes also minimize bandwidth costs by transferring data to AWS only as needed.
729: B is correct because predictive scaling uses machine learning to analyze each resource's daily and weekly historical workload trends and provisions capacity ahead of forecasted demand. Adding dynamic scaling with target tracking ensures the Auto Scaling group also responds in real time to live changes in utilization. Together the two policies form an automated scaling plan that satisfies both the forecast-based and reactive requirements.
730: A is correct because an ElastiCache for Redis cluster placed between the application and the Aurora cluster caches the results of the repeated read statements about delivery details, so those reads are served from memory instead of hitting the database. This directly alleviates the read load at a lower cost than continually adding Aurora read replicas or additional writer instances. Caching repeated identical reads is the standard and most cost-effective pattern for this workload.
731: C is correct because DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default, which means a read can return stale data that has not yet propagated to all storage nodes. Requesting strongly consistent reads guarantees the operation returns the most up-to-date data, resolving the issue of requests not returning the latest data. Since latency and other performance metrics are acceptable, consistency rather than capacity is the problem.
732: B is correct because AWS WAF inspects HTTP and HTTPS requests and uses managed rule groups to block common web exploits such as SQL injection, protecting the application as a fully managed service with minimal operational overhead. RDS parameter groups provide centralized configuration of database security settings without managing any infrastructure. This combination defends against web-based attacks at the application edge while the existing least-privilege credentials continue to govern database access.
733: B is correct because Amazon GuardDuty RDS Protection is a managed threat detection service that continuously analyzes Aurora database login activity to identify malicious behavior such as abnormal failed and incomplete login attempts. It requires no agents, log pipelines, or custom analysis, and it works across the member accounts of the organization, making it the most operationally efficient solution. Findings are surfaced automatically so security teams can act without building any aggregation infrastructure.
734: D is correct because a Direct Connect gateway allows a single Direct Connect connection to reach VPCs in multiple Regions through their virtual private gateways, providing scalable connectivity between both data centers and the VPCs in us-east-1 and eu-west-2. This avoids building full-mesh peering or VPN networks and centralizes the hybrid architecture, which reduces operational overhead. The non-overlapping CIDR blocks make routing across the Regions straightforward.
735: A is correct because Amazon Kinesis Data Streams can absorb large traffic spikes and preserves the order of records within each shard, meeting the requirement to process updates in order of receipt. AWS Lambda consumes the streams and scales automatically with the incoming volume, minimizing management overhead. Amazon DynamoDB provides a highly available, fully managed database for storing the processed updates.
736: B is correct because S3 Same-Region Replication automatically and continuously replicates log objects from each account's bucket to a centralized bucket in us-west-2, ensuring the data never leaves the Region. It is a native, fully managed S3 capability that requires no scripts, Lambda functions, or scheduled jobs, which minimizes operational overhead and cost.
737: C is correct because two-way replication among the buckets in all three Regions ensures that any video uploaded to any Region is automatically copied to the other Regions, keeping content globally consistent with no custom application logic. E is correct because an S3 Multi-Region Access Point exposes a single ARN that automatically routes both streaming and upload requests over the AWS global network to the lowest-latency Regional bucket, minimizing latency for developers and students near eu-west-2 and ap-southeast-1. Together these steps require only changing the application endpoints to the Multi-Region Access Point ARN, which is the fewest possible application changes.
738: B is correct because Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads over long distances by routing data through CloudFront edge locations near the user and over the AWS global backbone network into the S3 bucket, providing the lowest latency for content uploads from anywhere in the world. Since users consume most content within the Region where it is uploaded, storing the data in the S3 bucket keeps reads fast while Transfer Acceleration optimizes the upload path. It requires only a different endpoint and no additional infrastructure.
739: A is correct because an SNS topic receives the messages from the API Gateway REST API and fans them out to multiple SQS queues, and SNS subscription filter policies provide the message filtering so each target Lambda function receives only the messages it needs. The queues also decouple producers from consumers and add buffering for spikes. SNS and SQS are fully managed services, so this design meets the requirements with the least operational overhead.
740: A is correct because an S3 Inventory report can produce a list of the existing unencrypted objects, and an S3 Batch Operations job can process that list to encrypt those objects in place using SSE-C with the customer-provided key, handling millions of existing objects without writing custom code. Configuring the S3 default encryption feature to use SSE-C then ensures every future object is encrypted with the customer-provided key on upload. This combination addresses both existing and future objects.
